words.definition: Lasting only a brief while before passing or disappearing.
words.example: The hostel was full of transient guests who moved on after a single night.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'transit' — a passenger just passing through, never staying.

words.definition: Existing or useful for only a markedly short period.
words.example: Mayflies lead an ephemeral existence, dying within a day of hatching.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'ephemeros' (lasting a day) — picture a diary entry that expires by nightfall.

words.definition: Passing swiftly and gone almost at once.
words.example: She caught a fleeting glimpse of the deer before it bolted into the trees.
words.mnemonic: Fleeting = 'fleeing' — it runs away before you can hold it.

words.definition: Existing only briefly and soon over.
words.example: His fame proved transitory, forgotten within a single season.
words.mnemonic: Like a 'transit' station — you are only there in passing.

words.definition: Quickly fading from sight, sound, or memory.
words.example: The evanescent scent of the perfume was gone before she reached the door.
words.mnemonic: 'Vanish' hides inside it — e-VANESC-ent.

words.definition: Continuing forever without interruption.
words.example: The waterfall's perpetual roar never let the campers sleep.
words.mnemonic: Think of a 'perpetual-motion' machine that runs through all time.

words.definition: Continuing without any pause or break.
words.example: The incessant dripping of the tap kept him awake all night.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'cess' (cease) — it never ceases.

words.definition: Going on and on without ever stopping.
words.example: The ceaseless waves battered the cliff face for centuries.
words.mnemonic: 'Cease' + 'less' — literally without any stopping.

words.definition: Continuing strongly over a long stretch of time.
words.example: Their enduring friendship survived decades and three continents.
words.mnemonic: 'En-during' — it holds up 'during' all the hard times.

words.definition: Meant to last indefinitely without change or end.
words.example: After years of short contracts, she finally landed a permanent job.
words.mnemonic: 'Per-' (through) + 'man' — a man-made monument built to stay through time.

words.definition: Not moving, active, or changing.
words.example: The negotiations stayed static for weeks, with neither side budging.
words.mnemonic: A 'statue' is static — frozen in one pose.

words.definition: Full of energy, motion, and constant change.
words.example: The startup's dynamic culture reinvented itself every few months.
words.mnemonic: Think 'dynamite' — bursting with energy and force.

words.definition: To develop gradually into a different or better state.
words.example: Their garage band slowly evolved into a stadium-filling act.
words.mnemonic: 'E-volve' — picture a 'volume' knob turning up step by step.

words.definition: To change something completely in shape or nature.
words.example: A single coat of paint can transform a dingy room into a bright one.
words.mnemonic: 'Trans-' (across) + 'form' — carry a form across to a whole new shape.

words.definition: A complete change of form or character.
words.example: The caterpillar's metamorphosis into a butterfly amazed the children.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'meta' (change) + 'morph' (shape) — a changing of shape.

words.definition: Capable of being altered or transformed over time.
words.example: Unlike a printed book, a shared online document is mutable, so any editor can rewrite it.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'mutate' — like a virus that mutates, a mutable thing keeps shifting shape.

words.definition: Fixed and permanently incapable of being altered.
words.example: The laws of physics feel immutable: gravity behaves the same way today as it did a billion years ago.
words.mnemonic: 'im-' means 'not' + 'mutable' (changeable) — literally 'not changeable,' locked forever.

words.definition: A state of constant motion, shifting, and instability.
words.example: The startup's plans were in such flux that no one knew the strategy from one week to the next.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'flush' — water flushing and flowing, never staying still.

words.definition: Happening slowly by small steps over a long period.
words.example: Her recovery was gradual; she regained a little more strength each week rather than all at once.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'grade' — like a gentle grade on a ramp, you rise a little at a time.

words.definition: Sudden and unexpected, without any warning or transition.
words.example: The music's abrupt stop left the dancers frozen mid-step, unsure what had happened.
words.mnemonic: 'A-BRUPT' sounds like 'a rupture' — something that snaps open suddenly.

words.definition: No longer produced, used, or considered current.
words.example: Floppy disks are so obsolete that most new computers can't even read them anymore.
words.mnemonic: 'Oh, so late!' — it showed up too late to still be useful, already left behind.

words.definition: Old-fashioned and outdated compared with modern standards.
words.example: The office still ran on an antiquated fax system while competitors had moved to instant messaging.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'antique' — belongs in an antique shop, not in use today.

words.definition: To rot or break down slowly into a worse condition.
words.example: The abandoned barn began to decay, its roof caving in a little more each rainy season.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'cay' sounds like 'cake' left out — a cake going bad and falling apart.

words.definition: To become progressively worse in quality or condition.
words.example: Without regular maintenance, the roads deteriorate until they are full of potholes.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'deter' at the start — conditions get so bad they deter you from staying.

words.definition: To sink into a lower, worse, or less functional state.
words.example: The calm debate began to degenerate into shouting once tempers flared.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'generate' — instead of generating up, it generates downward into something worse.

words.definition: To wear away gradually through steady natural forces.
words.example: Years of crashing waves erode the cliff, carrying grains of rock into the sea.
words.mnemonic: 'E-rode' — the road got ridden over so many times it wore down to nothing.

words.definition: To waste away, especially from lack of use or nourishment.
words.example: After weeks in a cast, the muscles in his arm began to atrophy and grew visibly thinner.
words.mnemonic: 'A-trophy' — no trophy, no training; the unused muscle shrinks away.

words.definition: To dry up, shrivel, and lose freshness or vitality.
words.example: Left unwatered in the heat, the flowers began to wither and droop over the pot's edge.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'weather' — harsh weather makes a plant shrivel and fade.

words.definition: To decrease steadily in strength, amount, or quality.
words.example: Ticket sales continued to decline every year until the theater finally closed.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'cline' (lean/slope) — leaning downhill, sliding lower and lower.

words.definition: To return to an earlier, less developed or worse condition.
words.example: Under stress, the toddler would regress and start using baby talk he had outgrown.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (back) + 'gress' (step, as in 'progress') — stepping backward instead of forward.

words.definition: To grow into a fully developed adult or finished state over time.
words.example: The wine was left in oak barrels to mature for a decade before bottling.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ma-TOUR' — like a mother who has fully grown into her role after a long tour of life.

words.definition: To become fully grown and ready to eat, usually said of fruit.
words.example: We left the green tomatoes on the windowsill so they would ripen in the sun.
words.mnemonic: 'Rip' + 'en' — you rip open a fruit only when it's ready, and 'en' means to make it so.

words.definition: To grow strongly and succeed, especially under good conditions.
words.example: With plenty of rain and sun, the garden began to flourish in a riot of color.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'flour' in it — add flour and a bakery's business booms and grows.

words.definition: To do very well and grow vigorously, physically or financially.
words.example: Some cacti thrive in the desert where almost nothing else can survive.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'drive' — a driven person, full of energy, powers ahead and does great.

words.definition: To stop moving, growing, or developing and become dull or inactive.
words.example: Without new investment, the town's economy began to stagnate and shops closed.
words.mnemonic: A 'stagnant' pond — water that sits still, goes green, and never flows anywhere.

words.definition: To lose strength or vitality and remain in an unpleasant, neglected situation.
words.example: The proposal was left to languish in a drawer for years before anyone read it.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'anguish' — someone weak and suffering, slowly fading with no help.

words.definition: To bring something back to life, use, or awareness after it has faded.
words.example: A splash of cold water helped revive the fainting runner at the finish line.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (again) + 'vive' (life, as in 'vivid') — to give life again.

words.definition: To make someone or something feel young, fresh, or energetic again.
words.example: A week by the sea seemed to rejuvenate my exhausted grandmother completely.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'juven' (as in 'juvenile' = young) — to make young once more.

words.definition: To begin something again or extend it for a further period.
words.example: I had to renew my library card because it expired last month.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (again) + 'new' — to make new again.

words.definition: To bring something back to its original or former good condition.
words.example: Experts spent two years working to restore the faded fresco on the chapel ceiling.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' + 'store' — to put something back in the store, or back the way it was.

words.definition: A fresh rise or return of something after a period of decline.
words.example: Vinyl records have seen a surprising resurgence among younger music fans.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'surge' inside — a wave that had fallen suddenly surges upward again.

words.definition: A revival of interest, activity, or achievement, often in art or culture.
words.example: The neighborhood is enjoying a culinary renaissance, with new restaurants opening weekly.
words.mnemonic: French for 'rebirth' — think of the Renaissance, when art and learning were reborn.

words.definition: To return to a previous state, habit, or condition.
words.example: If you delete these edits, the document will revert to how it looked yesterday.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (back) + 'vert' (turn, as in 'U-turn') — to turn back to before.

words.definition: To fall back into a worse or former condition after improving.
words.example: The patient recovered well but began to relapse when she stopped her medication.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (again) + 'lapse' (a slip) — to slip back down again after doing better.

words.definition: The process of changing from one state or stage to another.
words.example: The transition from high school to college can feel overwhelming at first.
words.mnemonic: 'Trans-' means across — like 'transit' moving across, a shift across from one stage to the next.

words.definition: To keep switching between different opinions or choices, unable to decide.
words.example: She vacillated for an hour, picking up the dress and putting it back a dozen times.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'vase-ill-late' — picture a vase wobbling on a table's edge, never settling one way or the other.

words.definition: To rise and fall or change repeatedly in an irregular way.
words.example: Gas prices fluctuate so much that filling up costs me a different amount every week.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'flux', from Latin fluctus meaning 'wave' — picture waves heaving up and dropping down.

words.definition: To swing steadily back and forth between two points or states.
words.example: The fan's head oscillated slowly, sweeping a breeze across the whole room.
words.mnemonic: Think of an oscillating fan — 'oss-ill-ate' — the classic image of a head panning side to side.

words.definition: To hesitate or become unsteady, weakening in resolve or movement.
words.example: His voice wavered as he read the eulogy, threatening to break at every line.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'wave' inside it — a flag wavers, rippling unsteadily in a gusting wind.

words.definition: Lasting or recurring through many years; continuing without stopping.
words.example: Traffic is a perennial complaint here — every generation grumbles about the same jammed roads.
words.mnemonic: 'Per-' (through) + 'ennial' (from annus, year) — a perennial plant lives on through the years.

words.definition: Lasting only a very short time; over almost as soon as it begins.
words.example: There was a momentary flicker of the lights before the power steadied again.
words.mnemonic: 'Moment' sits right inside it — it lasts no longer than a single moment, a snap of the fingers.

words.definition: Relating to time, or to the physical world rather than spiritual matters.
words.example: The physicist studied the temporal order of events, mapping which one came before which.
words.mnemonic: 'Tempo' — the beat of time — hides inside it, and Latin 'tempus' means time.

words.definition: Continuing for a long time or constantly recurring, especially an illness or problem.
words.example: Her chronic back pain had bothered her every single day for over a decade.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'chronos' (time), like Father Time — a chronic condition drags on and on.

words.definition: Just coming into existence; still at a very early stage of development.
words.example: The nascent startup had only three employees and a whiteboard full of ideas.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'natal' and 'nativity' — nascent means freshly born.

words.definition: At an initial stage; starting to appear but not yet fully formed.
words.example: The doctor spotted an incipient infection before any real symptoms had shown.
words.mnemonic: Say 'in-SIP-ient' — take the first sip; it's only just getting started.

words.definition: At an early, undeveloped stage; not yet formed or matured.
words.example: The plan was still embryonic — a few scribbled notes rather than a real strategy.
words.mnemonic: Think 'embryo' — a tiny, unborn thing, undeveloped and just taking shape.

words.definition: Beginning to develop and showing signs of future promise or growth.
words.example: The budding pianist practiced four hours a day, dreaming of the concert stage.
words.mnemonic: Picture a flower bud about to open — a budding talent is on the verge of blooming.

words.definition: New and inexperienced; only recently started and not yet established.
words.example: The fledgling airline owned just two planes and flew to a single city.
words.mnemonic: A fledgling is a baby bird just growing feathers, testing its wings for the first time.

words.definition: In the process of coming into being or becoming noticeable and prominent.
words.example: Scientists watched an emergent pattern rise from the chaos of the raw data.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'emerge' — something emergent is rising into view, like a swimmer breaking the surface.

words.definition: The start or beginning of something, such as an organization or activity.
words.example: The club has welcomed dogs since its inception, when two friends founded it in a garage.
words.mnemonic: The film 'Inception' plants an idea at its very start — inception is the beginning point.

words.definition: The start or early stage of something, frequently something unpleasant or difficult.
words.example: At the onset of the storm, everyone scrambled to bring the chairs indoors.
words.mnemonic: Picture a film crew arriving 'ON SET' — that's when the shoot begins.

words.definition: The origin or point at which something first comes into being.
words.example: The genesis of the company was a late-night chat between two friends in a garage.
words.mnemonic: Genesis is the first book of the Bible — the story of how everything started.

words.definition: The arrival or coming of an important person, event, or thing.
words.example: The advent of the smartphone completely reshaped how people stay in touch.
words.mnemonic: An Advent calendar counts down the days to the arrival of Christmas.

words.definition: The death or ending of a person, institution, or activity.
words.example: Streaming services hastened the demise of the neighborhood video rental store.
words.mnemonic: Break it as 'de-' (down) + 'mise' — picture a king brought down from his throne forever.

words.definition: The process of falling out of use and becoming outdated or no longer wanted.
words.example: Planned obsolescence means gadgets are engineered to fail after just a few years.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'obsolete' inside it — like floppy disks that nobody can even read anymore.

words.definition: A small trace or sign of something that once existed but is now gone.
words.example: The crumbling stone wall was the last vestige of the ancient fortress.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'vest' — an old vest forgotten in the closet, a trace of a past style.

words.definition: An object or custom that has survived from a much earlier period.
words.example: The museum's prized relic was a jeweled cup from a medieval monastery.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'relinquere,' to leave behind — a relic is what the past left behind.

words.definition: A small part or quantity left after the rest is used or gone.
words.example: She stitched a colorful quilt entirely from remnants of old dresses.
words.mnemonic: You can see 'remain' hiding inside — what remains is a remnant.

words.definition: Remaining or left over after the greater part has been removed or dealt with.
words.example: Even after airing out the room, a residual smell of smoke clung to the curtains.
words.mnemonic: Shares its root with 'residue' — the residue that stubbornly stays behind.

words.definition: Something handed down from a predecessor or from earlier times.
words.example: Her grandmother's fearless generosity was a legacy she carried her whole life.
words.mnemonic: 'LEG-acy' — the leg-up your ancestors give you, passed down like a relay baton.

words.definition: Traditions, culture, and qualities passed down from previous generations.
words.example: The summer festival proudly celebrates the town's rich cultural heritage.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'inHERIT' inside it — heritage is everything you inherit from your ancestors.

words.definition: Following accepted customs and traditional ways rather than being original.
words.example: They opted for a conventional wedding, complete with a church and a white gown.
words.mnemonic: Think of a CONVENTION where everyone agrees on the same normal way of doing things.

words.definition: Never having happened, existed, or been done before.
words.example: Scientists recorded an unprecedented spike in ocean temperatures this year.
words.mnemonic: 'Un-' + 'precedent' — there is no precedent, nothing that came before it.

words.definition: Introducing fresh ideas, methods, or creative ways of doing things.
words.example: The startup's innovative app let users pay for coffee with a fingerprint.
words.mnemonic: 'In + nova' (Latin for new star) — bringing something brand new into the world.

words.definition: Belonging to or happening in the present time; modern.
words.example: The gallery specializes in contemporary art created within the last decade.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-' (with) + 'tempor' (time) — moving right along with the current times.

words.definition: The ancient past, especially the era of early civilizations before the Middle Ages.
words.example: The museum's pottery and coins date back to remote antiquity, long before Rome was founded.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'antique' + 'city' — picture an ancient city full of antiques from thousands of years ago.

words.definition: Belonging to an earlier time that is now over and finished.
words.example: Looking at the old photographs, she smiled at the fashions of a bygone era.
words.mnemonic: Break it into 'by-gone' — days that have gone by and won't come back.

words.definition: Present but hidden, not yet developed, active, or visible.
words.example: His latent talent for painting surfaced only after he retired and finally picked up a brush.
words.mnemonic: 'Late' + 'ent' — it's running LATE, waiting quietly to show up later.

words.definition: Temporarily inactive or asleep, but able to become active again later.
words.example: The volcano had lain dormant for centuries before it suddenly rumbled back to life.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'dormire' (to sleep) — same root as 'dormitory,' a place to sleep.

words.definition: In a quiet, still state of temporary rest or inactivity.
words.example: After the surgery the disease remained quiescent for years, showing no symptoms at all.
words.mnemonic: Starts like 'quiet' — a quiescent thing is quiet and resting.

words.definition: To keep something developing gradually until it is ready to emerge.
words.example: Startups come here to incubate their ideas, slowly building prototypes before any public launch.
words.mnemonic: Think of a hen on eggs in an INCUBATOR, patiently warming them until they hatch.

words.definition: To cause something to continue indefinitely, often a condition or belief.
words.example: Repeating those tired stereotypes only serves to perpetuate prejudice for another generation.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'perpetual' — to make something perpetual, going on and on forever.

words.definition: To keep something going or maintain it over a period of time.
words.example: A few granola bars were enough to sustain the hikers until they reached the next town.
words.mnemonic: 'Sus-' (up) + 'tain' (hold, as in 'retain') — to hold something up so it keeps going.

words.definition: To keep something in its original condition and protect it from harm.
words.example: They vacuum-sealed the documents to preserve them from moisture and decay.
words.mnemonic: Think of jam 'preserves' in a jar — sealed up and kept fresh for later.

words.definition: To establish something so firmly that it becomes very hard to change.
words.example: Years of favorable coverage helped entrench the party's grip on power.
words.mnemonic: Picture soldiers digging a TRENCH so deep they can't be dislodged — firmly dug in.

words.definition: Firmly fixed and hard to change, especially a habit or belief.
words.example: Politeness was so ingrained in him that he apologized even to the furniture he bumped into.
words.mnemonic: Like a stain worked deep into the GRAIN of wood — impossible to scrub out.

words.definition: To turn slowly into hardened stone-like remains within rock over ages.
words.example: Under the right conditions, a leaf can fossilize and leave a perfect imprint in the rock.
words.mnemonic: Think 'fossil' — a dinosaur bone hardened and stuck in the distant past.

words.definition: To turn matter into stone, or to freeze someone stiff with fear.
words.example: The sudden roar in the dark was enough to petrify the campers where they stood.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'petra' (rock) — the root in 'petroleum'; to turn to rock or freeze stiff.

words.definition: To harden into bone, or to become rigid and unwilling to change.
words.example: Without new members, the club's rules began to ossify into tradition no one dared question.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'os' = bone (as in 'osseous') — turn into bone, then stiff and set.

words.definition: To become clear, definite, and settled in form or thought.
words.example: During the long walk, her vague plans finally began to crystallize into a clear decision.
words.mnemonic: Picture scattered sugar molecules snapping into a sharp CRYSTAL — a fuzzy idea taking shape.
